text.p: The price of copper dropped almost US$100 a tonne in London in a sudden sell-off after it had seemed set on making a rally.

News of a big decline in copper stocks failed to bring in enough buying to overcome selling at the higher prices. And the extent of selling led some traders to speculate that banks may still be unwinding a hoard of copper built up by Sumitomo Corp.
Precious metals prices also fell, wheat prices eased on technical factors while oil dropped under pressure from speculators who suspected the recent bull run might be ending.
The CRB index was down 2.21 at 241.12 in late business.
Long liquidation following recent Chinese sales and talk that several shorts were expecting a downturn in copper prices prompted a selling spree during an active LME session.
The waves of selling negated falling LME warehouse stocks, with the market ignoring a 13,475-tonne fall which left total inventories at a six-year low of 132,350 tonnes.
Several traders suggested that long positions once belonging to Japan's Sumitomo Corp were still being sold into rallies, although others were unconvinced.
"To me it's a miracle this market isn't any higher. Some positions must still be around from the Sumitomo scandal," a senior trader said.

Some also heard that influential Montreal scrap metal dealer Herbie Black might be selling copper again. His sales last June contributed to a price rout in a market unerved by rumours, later confirmed, that Hamanaka was in trouble.
Three months delivery copper was last at $1,925, down from Monday's $2,016 close after ranging between $2,102 and $1,916.
Other metals, although ending lower, failed to match the declines in the copper market. "There has been no widespread liquidation as we await the next move in copper," a trader said.
Consumer buying helped underpin aluminium, aiding a recovery from an earlier dip below $1,400. It was last at $1,408, versus $1,415.50.

Zinc after recent investment fund buying slipped with copper to $1,042, a loss of $12. Lead was down $9 at $737, although trade interest ahead of the European U.S. winter was evident. Nickel in tandem with copper lost all of its recent gains and tumbled to $7,340, against $7,409. On Monday prices hit a high of $7,450.

New York precious metals futures ended sharply lower Tuesday, with fund and trade selling, taking the complex down to two year lows in December silver. "We saw every type of selling today - fund selling, trade selling, producer hedging, and locals selling on weak looking technicals," Credit Suisse New York vice president. COMEX December silver ended down 11.0 cents at $4.820 an ounce. COMEX December gold ended down $3.00 an ounce at $381.60, after seeing an intraday low at $381.50, testing last week's support level Spot gold bullion ended quoted $380.35/380.85, compared to the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $381.70 and the New York close Monday at $382.90/383.40.

NYMEX oil prices were lower with some traders believing the lows were in for the day ahead of the American Petroleum Institute's weekly data. December crude was off by 52 cents to $24.33 a barrel in late trading, after a rash of selling in the morning. Views were mixed about the market's broader direction.
CBOT wheat futures closed 2-3/4 cents per bushel higher to 3/4 cents lower with nearby months up on ideas that the marekt was oversold.
